title: Quantitative Chemistry
seo_title: Year 10 Science: Quantitative Chemistry Worksheets (GCSE Combined Science)
standard_text: Conservation of mass and balanced chemical equations; relative formula mass; mass changes when a reactant or product is a gas; chemical measurements and uncertainty; moles (higher tier) and amounts of substances in equations; using moles to balance equations; concentration of solutions in g/dm³.
meta_desc: Free Year 10 GCSE Combined Science worksheets on quantitative chemistry: conservation of mass, balancing equations, relative formula mass, moles, reacting masses and concentration in g/dm³. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Mass of reactants = mass of products.
key_sub: Mr is the sum of the atomic masses; concentration = mass ÷ volume in dm³.
body_html:
How to think about it

Atoms are not lost or made in a reaction.

  • Balanced equations have the same number of each atom on both sides.
  • Mr = the sum of the relative atomic masses. Moles = mass ÷ Mr.
  • Concentration (g/dm³) = mass (g) ÷ volume (dm³). 1 dm³ = 1,000 cm³.
Example

Mr of CO₂ (C = 12, O = 16)?

12 + 16 + 16

Answer: 44

Example

10 g in 250 cm³. Concentration?

250 cm³ = 0.25 dm³

10 ÷ 0.25

Answer: 40 g/dm³

Common mistakes

  • Thinking mass is lost when a gas forms.
  • Forgetting to multiply by the small numbers in a formula.
  • Using cm³ instead of dm³ in concentration.

faq.q: How do you calculate relative formula mass?
faq.a: Add up the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in the formula. For H₂SO₄: 2 × 1 + 32 + 4 × 16 = 98.
Divide the mass of solute in grams by the volume of solution in dm³. Convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1,000.

faq.q: Why does the mass change when magnesium burns?
faq.a: Oxygen from the air combines with the magnesium, so the product is heavier. The total mass of all the substances is still conserved.
